stories.title: 'Overwhelmingly biased': the EU observers' final report hands Zambia 13 recommendations, and the government replies that observers cannot see what the police can
stories.excerpt: The EU Election Observation Mission published its final report on the 13 August general elections on Tuesday 3 November: 13 recommendations, eight of them priority. It found a competitive choice and efficient polling staff, but late legal changes, police bias, cadreism and incumbency advantage that distorted the playing field, a state broadcaster that gave the ruling party over 90 per cent of political airtime, and a six-hour halt in counting and court closures that curtailed transparency. Information Minister Elvis Nkandu replied the same day.

image.label: Thirteen recommendations
image.caption: The EU Election Observation Mission published its final report on the 13 August 2026 general elections on Tuesday 3 November 2026; the government replied through Information Minister Elvis Nkandu the same day.

body: Nearly twelve weeks after Zambians voted, the European Union's observers have delivered their last word on the election. The final report of the EU Election Observation Mission, published on Tuesday 3 November, runs to 13 recommendations, eight of them labelled priority, and its conclusion is a balanced one: the election offered a genuine choice and was competently run on the day, but the conditions around it were not equal. The government's response, issued through the Minister of Information and Media, Elvis Nkandu, accepts the praise and contests much of the rest.

The mission was in the country from 29 June to 1 September at the government's invitation, led by the Member of the European Parliament Michael McNamara, and deployed 100 observers from 26 EU member states, Canada and Norway on election day. Its observers watched 39 polling stations open, voting in 419, counting in 38 and tabulation at 64 totalling centres.

On the positive side the report says the amended legal framework provided a broadly adequate basis for democratic elections, that the Electoral Commission of Zambia was well prepared, that candidate registration was inclusive and transparent and that voter registration used a new online portal. Election day itself was calm. The voters' roll certified on 4 May held 8,786,300 names, a quarter more than in 2021, though the Commission reached only half of its target of 3.5 million new registrations.

The criticism is directed at the surroundings. Reforms enacted about three months before polling created uncertainty; a law on political parties, which the Constitutional Court had ordered within 12 months, remains unenacted, and there is still no political finance law. The report records police bias, including disproportionate use of tear gas and blocked events, violence by what it calls groups traditionally associated with political movements that caused at least two deaths, and a presidential campaign timetable from which the President and Vice-President were exempt while other candidates could visit each province once, for five days. Women were about nine per cent of candidates; one of the 14 presidential candidates was a woman.

The mission's media monitoring is the sharpest finding. It describes the coverage of the state broadcaster as overwhelmingly biased, recording that the UPND received 96.2 per cent of political airtime on ZNBC television and 90.5 per cent on ZNBC radio, amid what it calls self-censorship linked to the cyber laws.

Two episodes after polling day carry the heaviest language. On 14 August the Commission suspended counting and the announcement of results across the country for about six hours; the report says the scale of the security concerns given for the decision was insufficiently explained, and that observers then saw tabulation deteriorate, with procedural omissions and weak safeguards. The Commission declared the presidential result on 18 August but, the report says, no full set of results has been posted publicly at polling-station level. The courts were then physically closed from 24 to 26 August, which took two of the seven days the Constitution allows for filing a presidential petition.

body.text: curtailed transparency and access to justice
body.attribution: Michael McNamara, Chief Observer, on the suspension of counting and the subsequent court closures, in the mission's statement of 3 November 2026

body: The eight priority recommendations are to revise the electoral law well before an election, to guarantee transparency throughout the process, to protect freedom of assembly and equal campaign opportunity and to end the Commission's role in issuing campaign timetables, to turn ZNBC into a genuine public service broadcaster, to align the cyber laws with international commitments on free expression, to guarantee observers unhindered access, to guarantee due process in electoral disputes, and to keep tabulation transparent with prompt online posting of polling-station results. The report notes that of the 22 recommendations its predecessor made in 2021, only one, an access-to-information law, was fully implemented.

Nkandu's statement, carried by the Zambian Observer on Tuesday, welcomes the mission's findings that voters had a competitive choice, that polling staff were efficient, that the legal framework was broadly adequate and that the Commission was well prepared. It then argues that the government was not given enough opportunity to supply the historical, institutional and security context, which it says leaves some findings incomplete.

On the late amendments, the statement says changing electoral law in an election year is not unprecedented in Zambia, citing reforms under Kenneth Kaunda, Frederick Chiluba's in 1996 and Edgar Lungu's in 2016, which introduced the 50-per-cent-plus-one threshold and the running mate, and it places the 2026 changes, including proportional representation, in that line. On ZNBC it says the broadcaster sells airtime to all parties on equal commercial terms, that its statutory duty includes informing citizens about the work of government, and that coverage of a sitting president is long-standing practice. On the security operations it says observers cannot see intelligence or law-enforcement investigations, and that some political actors and their supporters were under investigation for serious alleged crimes. It describes the media environment as vibrant and pluralistic and restates the government's commitment to constitutional rights.
The mission's statement says the EU stands ready to support Zambia in implementing the recommendations. The full report is published on the website of the European External Action Service.

body.confirmed: The final report and its 13 recommendations were published on 3 November 2026 by the EU EOM; the airtime figures, the six-hour suspension of counting on 14 August and the court closure of 24 to 26 August are the mission's own findings, as set out in the report and its statement. The government's response is a statement by Information Minister Elvis Nkandu carried by the Zambian Observer on 3 November.
body.unverified: Whether the Electoral Commission or the courts will respond to the report separately; whether any of the recommendations will be taken up by the government or Parliament, which the government's statement does not address; and the mission's characterisation of the reasons for the 14 August suspension, which the Commission has not answered in the reporting read today.

stories.title: A day before the declaration, Kasonde Mwenda asks the High Court to halt the Mandevu process, arguing the Commission had no power to scrap the August poll and order a new one
stories.excerpt: Economic Freedom Fighters president Kasonde Mwenda has applied for leave to seek judicial review of the Electoral Commission's handling of Mandevu, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday 3 November. His application, stamped on Monday, argues that no law allowed the Commission to abandon the 13 August election in the constituency and call a fresh one, and asks for Thursday's election to be stayed. Neither report says any order has been granted. The Commission expects to declare the UPND's Adrian Banda elected on Thursday.

image.label: Mandevu goes to court
image.caption: Kasonde Mwenda's application for leave to seek judicial review of the Electoral Commission's decisions on Mandevu was stamped at the Lusaka High Court on 2 November 2026, three days before the by-election date.

body: The Mandevu by-election, which has already lost its ballot, may now gain a court case. Kasonde Mwenda, the president of the Economic Freedom Fighters, has asked the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Electoral Commission of Zambia's decisions on the constituency and for a stay of the election set for Thursday 5 November, according to reports in Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer on Tuesday.

The application was filed ex parte at the Principal Registry in Lusaka and stamped on Monday 2 November, under case number 2026/HTR/1316, Zambia Monitor reports. The Commission is the first respondent and the Attorney-General the second. It is brought under Order 53 of the Rules of the Supreme Court and cites several articles of the Constitution.

Mwenda's case goes to the root of the by-election rather than to the withdrawals that emptied it. He challenges the Commission's decision of 28 August to abandon the earlier process in Mandevu, together with the later notices and directions for a fresh poll. His position, as reported, is that the Commission acted beyond its mandate and took to itself a power that belongs to the High Court: the power to set aside an election. In the words Zambia Monitor quotes from the application, there is no legal provision or authority empowering the Commission to take the action it has taken.

He asks for the election to be stayed until the court has resolved the legal questions. The Zambian Observer notes that its report describes a filing only and that nothing in it indicates the court has granted an order stopping the poll.

The Commission's own account of August, as the Zambian Observer set it out last week, is that criminals attacked the constituency's results-tallying centre on the night of the general election, destroyed data transmission equipment and stole election documents, rendering the process null and void; soldiers were deployed. Before the disruption the seat had been held by the UPND's Christopher Shakafuswa, and the contest was between Jean Kapata for the Resolute Party on the Tonse Alliance ticket and Adrian Banda, then an independent. Banda later joined the UPND and was adopted as its candidate for the rerun.

That rerun has since dissolved. Three candidates wrote to the Commission to withdraw: the former Lusaka mayor Daniel Chisenga, who was standing for the Forum for Democracy and Development on the Tonse ticket, the independent Daniel Daka, and Ntazana Muntungwa of the Leadership Movement. With one valid candidate left, the Commission will declare Banda elected rather than hold a vote. The same has happened in Lumezi North and in the Mbala mayoral by-election, where Felix Mulwanda of the UPND is to be declared mayor on Thursday after his only rival withdrew.

Voting does go ahead on Thursday in six wards in five districts, Commissioner Zevyanji Sinkala told poll staff in training at Lwingishi Ward in Mansa on Saturday, News Diggers reported; the UPND is unopposed in five others, Maako, Siluwe, Upangoma, Mulimambango and Simanvwa.

On Wednesday morning News Diggers devoted its editorial to the walkovers, arguing that the Commission may be following the 2016 regulations to the letter but that procedural compliance does not answer the question of how the withdrawals came about, and calling for the Anti-Corruption Commission to investigate. Whether the High Court entertains Mwenda's application before Thursday is the first thing to watch.

stories.title: Seven days to answer: M'membe asks the Law Association to defend the two-term limit, call a special general meeting and say whether tenure can change without a referendum
stories.excerpt: Socialist Party president Fred M'membe wrote to the Law Association of Zambia on Monday 2 November asking it to defend Article 106 of the Constitution, which bars anyone who has twice held the presidency from standing again, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer reported. He cites a petition to Parliament on 28 October seeking removal of the limit, the 2025 amendment that removed term limits for mayors, and public calls for President Hichilema to stay beyond 2031, and proposes that LAZ revive the church and civic coalition of 2001.

image.label: Article 106
image.caption: Fred M'membe's letter to the Law Association of Zambia on presidential term limits is dated 2 November 2026; a petition seeking removal of the limit was presented to Parliament on 28 October.

body: The argument over whether Zambia's presidency should stay limited to two terms has moved from the floor of Parliament to the lawyers. Fred M'membe, president of the Socialist Party, wrote on Monday 2 November to the president of the Law Association of Zambia asking the association to state publicly where it stands on Article 106 of the Constitution and to convene an extraordinary general meeting of its members on any proposal to amend it, Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer reported on Tuesday. He has asked for a written reply within seven days and says he will publish both the letter and the answer.

The trigger, as the letter sets it out, is the petition presented to the National Assembly on Wednesday 28 October by the Zambia Youth Organisations Consortium through the nominated MP Francis Kope, which seeks the removal of presidential term limits, together with public calls from officials and supporters of the ruling party for President Hakainde Hichilema to remain in office after 2031. The consortium's case, when it first petitioned the Assembly in September, was put by its vice-chairperson Boas Kanyama: that the ballot should be the only instrument through which citizens hire and fire their leaders.

M'membe's letter rests on three points. First, that the Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025 has already removed term limits for mayors and council chairpersons, which he presents as a precedent for what might follow. Second, that Article 79 requires a two-thirds majority of the National Assembly to amend the Constitution, and that the Constitutional Court's judgment of June 2025 on Bill 7 stressed the need for public consultation. Third, that a change to presidential tenure should not rest on a parliamentary majority alone, and he asks LAZ to say whether such a change should proceed without a national referendum.

He proposes that the association engage the Zambia Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Council of Churches in Zambia, the Evangelical Fellowship of Zambia, the NGOCC and the other bodies that worked together under the Oasis Forum in 2001. The Socialist Party, he writes, would join such a platform without seeking to lead it.

body.attribution: Fred M'membe, in his letter of 2 November 2026 as quoted by Zambia Monitor, saying the Socialist Party was not asking the association to adopt any party's position

body: Neither report carries a response from the Law Association, from the government or from the consortium, and neither describes any government proposal to amend Article 106. What exists is a petition before Parliament, and the letters and statements that have followed it.

stories.title: Sixty-forty and US$213 million over two phases: the IDC and a Beijing firm sign the ZAMVAX joint venture, starting with 20 million cholera doses a year filled in Lusaka South
stories.excerpt: The Industrial Development Corporation and Jijia (Beijing) International Medical Technology signed a joint venture agreement on Monday 2 November to develop ZAMVAX Limited, a vaccine maker to be built in the Lusaka South Multi-Facility Economic Zone, with the IDC holding 60 per cent. Phase one, an oral cholera vaccine fill-and-finish line costing about US$24.13 million and built for up to 20 million doses a year, uses imported bulk antigen; a second phase of about US$189 million would add local antigen production.

image.label: ZAMVAX, phase one
image.caption: The Industrial Development Corporation and Jijia (Beijing) International Medical Technology signed the ZAMVAX joint venture agreement in Lusaka on Monday 2 November 2026; the first plant is to be built in Lusaka South.

body: The cholera vaccine plant planned for Lusaka South now has its corporate form. The Industrial Development Corporation and Jijia (Beijing) International Medical Technology Limited signed a joint venture agreement in Lusaka on Monday 2 November to develop ZAMVAX Limited, the Times of Zambia, Zambia Monitor and News Diggers reported. The IDC will own 60 per cent of the company and the Chinese partner 40.

The IDC's chief executive, Cornwell Muleya, put the total investment at about US$213 million, News Diggers reports, in two phases: US$24.13 million for the first and US$189 million for the second. The Times of Zambia rounds the project to US$200 million. Muleya cited the country's recurring cholera epidemics as the reason for starting with that vaccine.

Phase one is a fill-and-finish facility in the Lusaka South Multi-Facility Economic Zone: imported bulk oral cholera vaccine antigen will be filled, finished, packaged and quality-controlled locally, at a designed capacity of up to 20 million doses a year. Phase two, if it proceeds, would add production of the antigen itself, giving end-to-end manufacture of cholera vaccine in Zambia. The partners have also spoken of possible later expansion into paediatric and animal vaccines, subject to feasibility studies, financing and regulatory approval, Zambia Monitor reports.

The agreement builds on an agreement signed in 2024 and sets out the governance, funding and implementation terms. Muleya said the aim is for Zambia to become self-sufficient in cholera vaccine and eventually to supply a wider range of vaccines to the region, with technology transfer and workforce training built in; he placed the project within the Grow Zambia Agenda. Jijia's general manager, Su Yong Lin, described the partnership as support for Zambia's health sector and for health security across Africa.

body.title: ZAMVAX at a glance
items: Partners: Industrial Development Corporation (60%) and Jijia (Beijing) International Medical Technology (40%)
Phase one: oral cholera vaccine fill-and-finish, about US$24.13 million, up to 20 million doses a year, Lusaka South MFEZ
Phase two: local antigen production, about US$189 million (News Diggers); total about US$213 million
Next steps: financing, site preparation, technical agreements, workforce development and regulatory approvals; groundbreaking expected in the coming weeks

body: What is not yet public is how the first US$24 million will be financed and on what terms, or when the first locally filled dose might reach a clinic. The company's next steps, as the partners list them, are to secure financing, prepare the site, conclude technical agreements, train the workforce and obtain regulatory approvals.

stories.title: Oversubscribed by K3.5 billion: the Bank of Zambia formally closes the K5 billion drought and load-shedding facility, and says borrowers must still get the benefit of any rate cut
stories.excerpt: The Bank of Zambia has closed its Stability and Resilience Facility, the K5 billion line opened in December 2024 for businesses hit by the 2023/24 drought and the power shortages that followed, Zambia Monitor reported on Tuesday 3 November. Applications reached K8.5 billion against the K5 billion available; the access window, extended once from 31 December 2025, closed on 31 March 2026, by which date the bank's own journal had recorded full utilisation. The bank says the facility largely met its objectives and that it will keep monitoring the loans.

image.label: K5 billion, fully drawn
image.caption: The Bank of Zambia's K5 billion Stability and Resilience Facility, opened in December 2024 for drought- and load-shedding-hit businesses, reached full utilisation by 31 March 2026 and has now been formally closed.

body: The emergency credit line the central bank opened at the depth of the drought has been wound up. In a statement reported by Zambia Monitor on Tuesday 3 November, the Bank of Zambia said its K5 billion Stability and Resilience Facility had been closed, having been fully taken up, with applications worth K8.5 billion received for the K5 billion on offer.

The facility was launched in December 2024, after the 2023/24 El Niño drought cut food production and the water behind the hydro-electric dams, to protect the stability of the financial system and keep credit flowing to the businesses the drought and the power cuts had hurt most. The money was channelled through banks and other financial service providers, which on-lent it to farms and to micro, small and medium enterprises affected by load shedding, at concessional rates, with a repayment moratorium and tenors of up to seven years.

According to the bank's assistant director for communications, Besnat Mwanza, the funds went to agriculture, energy solutions and other productive activity, including climate-smart farming, irrigation, waste management and water reticulation. The bank's own journal, the Zambanker, had reported in its March edition that the facility reached full utilisation on 31 March 2026 and described it as having completed its primary mandate of injecting liquidity into the economy in support of productivity and energy security, with allocations to energy, agriculture, forestry and manufacturing.
The access window was originally 12 months to 31 December 2025 and was extended to 31 March 2026, the statement says. Mwanza said the bank was satisfied the facility had largely met its objectives.

One condition survives the closure. Financial service providers must pass any cut in the Monetary Policy Rate on to their SRF borrowers: the rate on an advance falls when the policy rate is cut but does not rise when it is raised. The bank says it will continue to monitor both how the disbursed money is used and how the loans perform.

The closure comes two days before the 2027 budget. The same edition of the Zambanker recorded the kwacha closing 2025 at K22.80 to the dollar after three quarters of appreciation, which the bank credited to improved foreign exchange supply, higher copper prices, the rating upgrades and progress under the IMF programme.

stories.title: A spirit-like smell at Kafue: the ZRA stops three trucks carrying 119,500 litres of ethanol declared at Chirundu as paraffin, and says the false entry would have cost K5.8 million
stories.excerpt: Officers of the Zambia Revenue Authority's Mobile Enforcement Unit stopped three super-link trucks at the Kafue checkpoint carrying 478 drums of 250 litres each that had been entered at the Chirundu One Stop Border Post as paraffin, News Diggers and Zambia Monitor reported on Tuesday 3 November. An inspection found a smell inconsistent with paraffin; laboratory tests at the Makeni Enforcement Centre confirmed ethanol. The authority puts the revenue at stake at about K5.8 million and warns that false declarations carry seizure and prosecution.

image.label: 478 drums at Kafue
image.caption: The Zambia Revenue Authority intercepted 119,500 litres of ethanol declared as paraffin at the Kafue checkpoint; the consignment had entered Zambia through the Chirundu One Stop Border Post.

body: Three articulated trucks, 478 drums and one description that did not match the cargo: the Zambia Revenue Authority says its Mobile Enforcement Unit has intercepted 119,500 litres of ethanol that had been declared as paraffin, averting a potential loss of about K5.8 million in revenue, News Diggers and Zambia Monitor reported on Tuesday 3 November.

The consignment had been entered at the Chirundu One Stop Border Post on the Zimbabwe frontier. It was at the Kafue checkpoint, on the road to Lusaka, that officers questioned the description of the goods. A physical inspection raised the first doubt, the authority's corporate communications manager, Oliver Nzala, said: the liquid had a spirit-like smell inconsistent with paraffin. The trucks were impounded and escorted to the Makeni Enforcement Centre, where samples were taken; laboratory results confirmed ethanol.

The declared description of imported goods determines their tariff classification and therefore the duties and taxes payable, Nzala said, which is why a false declaration deprives the Treasury of revenue and distorts competition against importers who declare correctly. The K5.8 million is the authority's figure for the revenue that would have been lost on this consignment had the declaration stood.

False declarations are an offence under the Customs and Excise Act, Chapter 322 of the Laws of Zambia, and offenders risk seizure of the goods and prosecution, Nzala said. He urged importers and clearing agents to make sure their declarations match the goods and the supporting documents, advised anyone uncertain of a classification to seek clarification from the authority before declaring, and asked the public to report suspected smuggling to the nearest ZRA office.

Neither report names the importer or the clearing agent, and neither says whether anyone has been charged. The authority's account describes the trucks as impounded and the matter as under its enforcement process; what follows, whether a penalty, forfeiture or a prosecution, has not been reported.

stories.title: The witness waits: Archbishop Banda's trial is put off to Friday 6 November because the prosecutor who was to cross-examine is before the Solwezi High Court, 700 kilometres away
stories.excerpt: The trial of Lusaka's Catholic Archbishop, Alick Banda, on a charge of possessing property reasonably believed to have been unlawfully obtained did not open on Tuesday 3 November as scheduled. Deputy Chief State Advocate Mercy Lungu told the Lusaka Magistrates' Court that the prosecutor assigned to the case was before the Solwezi High Court, and Senior Resident Magistrate Mwandu Nakazwe adjourned to Friday 6 November, saying the prosecution had to be present to answer a fresh defence motion. The archbishop denies the charge and is on K80,000 bail.

image.label: Adjourned to Friday
image.caption: The trial of Archbishop Alick Banda at the Lusaka Magistrates' Court, due to open on Tuesday 3 November 2026, was adjourned to Friday 6 November before the first witness was called.

body: The trial of Archbishop Alick Banda was due to open on Tuesday 3 November at the Lusaka Magistrates' Court. It did not. Before the first prosecution witness could be called, the State asked for more time, and Senior Resident Magistrate Mwandu Nakazwe adjourned the case to Friday 6 November, the Times of Zambia and the Zambian Observer reported.

The reason, as Deputy Chief State Advocate Mercy Lungu explained it to the court, was geography. The prosecutor assigned to cross-examine was in Solwezi, more than 700 kilometres away, attending to a matter before the Solwezi High Court; the notice of that hearing, the State said, had arrived after the trial dates in Lusaka were fixed. The magistrate granted the adjournment, saying the prosecution needed to be present to respond to a fresh motion from the defence, and that it was in the interest of justice to allow it.

The archbishop, who is 62, faces one count under Section 319 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87: being found in possession of property reasonably believed to have been stolen or unlawfully obtained. The particulars allege that between 22 April 2021 and 27 December 2023 he had in his possession a blue Toyota Hilux, registration ALF 7734, suspected to have been unlawfully obtained from the Zambia Revenue Authority. The vehicle is reported to be one of about 22 that the authority is alleged to have disposed of irregularly, which is the subject of a wider investigation. He has pleaded not guilty and is on K80,000 bail with three sureties.

News Diggers reported in mid-October, when Nakazwe set the trial for 3 November, that the particulars then gave the period as April 2021 to September 2023; the Times of Zambia and the Zambian Observer both give 27 December 2023 in their reports of Tuesday's hearing.

body.confirmed: That the trial did not open on 3 November, that the State sought the adjournment because its prosecutor was before the Solwezi High Court, and that the matter returns on Friday 6 November, as reported by the Times of Zambia and the Zambian Observer. The charge, the vehicle and the bail terms are as reported by both outlets and by News Diggers in October.
body.unverified: What the defence's fresh motion seeks, which neither report describes; whether the prosecution witnesses will be available on Friday; and the archbishop's guilt or innocence, which is for the court. He has pleaded not guilty.

body: Friday's sitting will show whether the State's witnesses are ready and what the defence motion is.

stories.title: Two sedition files, one Monday: Nakacinda is put on his defence over the 'genocide' maize remarks, and surety Mulenga Fube must pay K100,000 or serve six months over Binwell Mpundu
stories.excerpt: The Lusaka Magistrates' Court found on Monday 2 November that Raphael Nakacinda, secretary-general of a faction of the Patriotic Front, has a case to answer on one count of seditious practices over an August 2024 broadcast in which he allegedly accused the government of genocide by importing maize contaminated with aflatoxins; his defence opens on 22 December. In the same court, Magistrate Webster Milumbe ordered Mulenga Fube, a surety for former Nkana MP Binwell Mpundu, to pay a K100,000 bond or serve six months after he could not say where Mpundu is.

image.label: Two sedition files
image.caption: The Lusaka Magistrates' Court ruled on Monday 2 November 2026 that Raphael Nakacinda has a case to answer for seditious practices, and ordered Binwell Mpundu's surety Mulenga Fube to pay K100,000 or serve six months.

body: Monday was a day of reckoning in two of the sedition cases working through the Lusaka Magistrates' Court, one at the end of the prosecution's evidence and one at the point where a surety is made to answer for the accused.

Raphael Nakacinda, secretary-general of a faction of the Patriotic Front, must now defend himself against a charge of seditious practices, Magistrate Mwandu Nakazwe ruled on Monday 2 November, Zambia Monitor and News Diggers reported. The charge concerns remarks he is alleged to have made on Millennium Radio on 21 August 2024, that the government was committing genocide against its own citizens by importing maize and mealie-meal contaminated with aflatoxins. The magistrate found that the prosecution had established a prima facie case.

His lawyer, Maluza Chongola, told the court that Nakacinda will give sworn evidence and call ten witnesses. The court adjourned to 22 December for the defence to begin and directed that it conclude by February 2027. A finding of a case to answer is not a finding of guilt: it means the evidence, untested by the defence, is enough to require one. Zambia Monitor's report attributes the detail of the ruling to ZNBC.

body.text: Fube: a bond or six months

body: Across the same building, the long search for Binwell Mpundu reached his sureties. The former Nkana MP faces one count of seditious practices over a Facebook post of 30 December 2024 in which he allegedly urged the public and politicians to acquire firearms for self-defence, the Zambian Observer reported. He failed to appear in October, when Magistrate Webster Milumbe issued a bench warrant against him for the second time; the first, in July, was revoked after the court accepted his explanation, News Diggers reported. The court summoned his two sureties, the former Chilubi MP Mulenga Fube and the former Kamfinsa MP Christopher Kang'ombe, to produce him or account for his whereabouts.

Fube could not. He was brought from police custody, where he had been held since the previous Saturday over what the Zambian Observer describes as an undisclosed offence, and told the court that he did not know where Mpundu was, that Mpundu had not disclosed his exact location in their last conversation, and that he needed time to raise money. Milumbe ordered him to pay a K100,000 bond or serve six months in prison, and said he may pay the bond once he raises it. Kang'ombe, who had sent word through Mpundu's lawyer Leon Lemba that he was unwell, has until 23 November to explain Mpundu's whereabouts.

Mpundu himself has not been reported as found or arrested. The bench warrant stands, and the sedition charge against him is untried; nothing in the reporting read today suggests any finding against him on it.

stories.title: Four from four, by a point: Munali Suns hold off a Harare Kings fourth-quarter comeback to win 70–69 at NASDEC and sit alone at the top of Group E
stories.excerpt: A day after beating Botswana's Dolphins by 40, Munali Suns needed every one of their 70 points to see off Harare Kings 70–69 on Monday 2 November in the Road to BAL 2027 group in Lusaka. Comfortable for most of the game, the hosts watched the Zimbabweans cut the lead to one in the final quarter, with Ofure Ujagudhele's three-pointer among the shots that kept them in it, News Diggers reports. The win leaves Munali at four wins from four with a points difference of plus 56, ahead of Ferroviário da Beira and Dolphins, both three and one.

image.label: Munali 70, Harare 69
image.caption: Munali Suns beat Harare Kings 70–69 at the NASDEC Sports Complex in Lusaka on Monday 2 November 2026, their fourth win from four in Group E of the Road to BAL 2027.

body: The 40-point stroll against Dolphins on Sunday was followed by a one-point scramble on Monday. Munali Suns beat Harare Kings 70–69 at the NASDEC Sports Complex on Monday 2 November to go four from four in Group E of the Road to BAL 2027 qualifiers, News Diggers reported, but only after a fourth-quarter comeback by the Zimbabwean side had turned a comfortable evening into a nervous one.

Munali led for most of the game. The visitors, who had lost 72–77 to Dolphins and 71–98 to Beira earlier in the week and had only a 66–47 win over Soweto Panthers to show for their trip, found their shooting late. Ofure Ujagudhele's three-pointer was one of the scores that brought them within reach, and News Diggers' report names Elijah Mukelebai and Douglas Kandulu among the Munali players who had to answer. The hosts held on by the single point.

The result leaves Munali alone at the top of the group on four wins from four, with 332 points scored and 276 conceded, a difference of plus 56, according to the standings published by The BAL Report. Ferroviário da Beira, whom Munali beat 87–85 on Saturday, are second at three and one with the group's best points difference, plus 83, after their 110–81 win over Bravehearts on Monday. Dolphins are also three and one despite a difference of minus 24, after beating Soweto Panthers 63–56. Harare Kings and Bravehearts have one win each; Soweto Panthers have none.

The qualifying page of The BAL Report says only that the clubs that qualify from the group go on to the Basketball Africa League in 2027 and does not state how many advance from Group E or on what tie-break. What is certain is that the Lusaka club has won all four of its games in the group so far, and that its last fixture, against Soweto Panthers, will decide whether it finishes unbeaten.

stories.title: An uncle in WITCH and a 16-track answer: Sampa the Great's 'Nu Zamrock' takes the psychedelic rock of 1970s Zambia and rebuilds it with Mag44, Sia and a family interview
stories.excerpt: Sampa the Great released 'Nu Zamrock', her third studio album, on Friday 30 October through Loma Vista Recordings, Zambia Monitor reported on Tuesday. The 16 tracks, about 37 minutes, fold hip-hop, rock and soul into the Zamrock sound of the 1970s, and the record opens with an interview with her uncle George Kunda, known as Groovy Joe, a founding member of WITCH. Mag44 and Solomon Moyo produced with her and Cadenza; Sia, KAMAUU, Mwanjé and Nicole Gumbe are the guests. She plays two sold-out shows at Blue Note London on Wednesday.

image.label: Nu Zamrock
image.caption: Sampa the Great's third studio album, 'Nu Zamrock', was released on 30 October 2026 through Loma Vista Recordings; its 16 tracks draw on the Zambian psychedelic rock of the 1970s.

body: The Zambian-Australian rapper and singer Sampa the Great has made the record her family history was waiting for. 'Nu Zamrock', released on Friday 30 October through Loma Vista Recordings and reported by Zambia Monitor on Tuesday 3 November, is her third studio album, after 'The Return' in 2019 and 'As Above, So Below' in 2022, and its 16 tracks, running about 37 minutes, set hip-hop, rock, soul and Zambian rhythm inside the sound of Zamrock, the psychedelic rock that Zambian bands made in the 1970s.

The album grew out of a discovery. While reconnecting with relatives in Zambia, Sampa learned that her uncle, George Kunda, known as Groovy Joe, was a founding member of WITCH, one of the bands that defined the movement. The record opens with an interview with him about the band's history, so that the genre's past introduces its present.

Sampa executive-produced the album with Cadenza, and the Zambian producers Magnus 'Mag44' Mando and Solomon Moyo worked on it with them. The guests are Sia, on 'Supernova', KAMAUU, on 'Star', Mwanjé and Nicole Gumbe. Loma Vista's own description of the record is that it is fierce and uncompromising.
She previewed the material at festivals in Australia in October and plays a sold-out double show at Blue Note London on Wednesday 4 November, the first dates with the album out.

For Zambian listeners the interest is partly in the lineage. An album that puts a founding member of WITCH on its first track, made with producers from Lusaka and released on an American label, carries the sound of the 1970s to an audience that Zambia Monitor notes has already sold out two nights in London.

sources.title: Sampa The Great releases 'Nu Zamrock' album inspired by family roots

analysis.title: Thirteen recommendations and a track record of one: what the EU report can and cannot do
analysis.body: The EU mission's final report has no legal force, and both sides know it. Its weight comes from the detail: airtime measured to a decimal point, a six-hour suspension of counting that the mission says was never adequately explained, courts closed for two of the seven petition days. The government's reply does not dispute those facts so much as their framing. It says election-year amendments have precedents going back to Kaunda, that ZNBC's commercial airtime is open to all and its duty to report government is statutory, and that observers cannot see what investigators can. Those are arguments about context, and its complaint that it was not asked for that context is its strongest card. The weakest point in the government's position is the one the report puts in a single line: of 22 recommendations made in 2021, one was implemented. The political parties law the Constitutional Court ordered is still not enacted. What to watch is not a reply to Brussels but three domestic tests: whether the Electoral Commission publishes polling-station results, whether the budget session finds time for the parties and political finance bills, and whether the cyber laws are touched at all.

analysis.title: Thursday: a declaration under challenge, a bail ruling due, and six wards that will vote
analysis.body: Thursday 5 November was meant to be by-election day. It has become something more complicated. In Mandevu the Electoral Commission intends to declare Adrian Banda elected without a vote, and Kasonde Mwenda has asked the High Court to stop it, not because of the withdrawals but because, he argues, the Commission had no power to cancel the August election in the first place. His application was stamped on Monday; nothing reported so far says a judge has granted leave, let alone a stay, and unless that changes the declaration goes ahead. At the High Court, meanwhile, the constitutional bail application of Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 16 others returns at nine o'clock, after a court that has said it will allow no further adjournment. And in six wards in five districts, people will queue and vote. News Diggers' editorial on Wednesday argues that lawful walkovers still need explaining and wants the Anti-Corruption Commission to look at how they came about. The unresolved question is institutional: who, if anyone, examines a withdrawal once the Commission has accepted the letter.

analysis.title: Two days to the budget: the drought money is spent, and the reserves argument is back
analysis.body: The Bank of Zambia's closure of its K5 billion Stability and Resilience Facility is a tidy end to the drought emergency: oversubscribed by K3.5 billion, fully drawn by March, concessional terms that still ratchet down with the policy rate. It is also a reminder that the easy liquidity is gone just as the next shock arrives through the fuel pump. Gertrude Imenda, a nominated UPND MP, told News Diggers it would be perfectly in order to use some of the country's US$6.5 billion in reserves to steady the kwacha and cushion fuel; Vice-President Nalumango had told Parliament on Friday that the government has no such intention. Friday's budget is where that argument gets settled, in the exchange-rate assumption, the fuel levies and the size of the deficit. One more item belongs on the watch list: Zambia Monitor, citing Access Bank commentary, reports that the Africa Finance Corporation is asking Zambia and Angola for initial viability-gap funding for the Lobito railway after expected commitments from international partners did not materialise. If that is confirmed, the US$3 to 5 billion line Lusaka has been counting on will need a line of its own in someone's budget.
